claims.text: The starting material is an initially single-phase, disordered FCC compositionally complex alloy.
Annealing can transform a disordered FCC matrix into a hierarchical three-phase structure containing FCC, κ, and L12 phases.
The annealing-induced κ and L12 regions are nanoscale.
Brittle behavior emerges when hierarchical κ and L12 ordering exceeds a critical volume fraction.
Hierarchical κ and L12 ordering suppresses dislocation multiple slip and stacking-fault formation.
Overordering reduces strain-hardening capacity.
Ordered/disordered interfaces localize stress.
The ordering-induced changes cause a transition from homogeneous plastic flow to brittle fracture.
The proposed brittle transition can occur without grain-boundary segregation or intergranular precipitation.
In the as-quenched single-phase state, dislocation activity, multiple slip, and stacking-fault formation enable uniform plastic deformation.
Long-range ordered phases in HEAs and MEAs are generally associated with poor ductility because of their brittle complex structures and bonding.
Annealed, hierarchically ordered material will have lower tensile ductility than the single-phase baseline.
Annealed, hierarchically ordered material will have lower toughness than the single-phase baseline.
Annealed, hierarchically ordered material will show more brittle fracture morphology than the single-phase baseline.
The proposed ordering-controlled mechanism operates at intermediate temperatures of approximately 400–800°C.
The proposed mechanism applies at conventional engineering strain rates.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under cryogenic or extreme loading conditions because mechanisms such as twinning may dominate.
The critical ordered-phase volume fraction and spatial distribution required for brittle failure are unknown.
Identically composed quenched and annealed samples tested at 600°C provide a controlled comparison of the single-phase and ordered states.
Equal or greater ductility, strain hardening, and fracture toughness in the ordered sample relative to the single-phase control would falsify the proposed embrittlement mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says κ and L12 ordering suppresses multiple slip and stacking-fault activity and reduces strain hardening, whereas the designated supporting evidence reports that κ-phase multiple slip and stacking faults, together with mechanisms in L12 and FCC regions, enhance strain hardening and ductility.

The predicted outcome is lower ductility and brittle fracture after hierarchical ordering, but the cited same-study evidence reports 30% room-temperature ductility and an excellent strength–ductility combination in the hierarchically ordered material.
